Before the answer could form, deep thuds began rolling up through the ground—booming, ground-shaking footfalls that came pacing through the trees like something enormous running, T-Rex through the underbrush, close and getting closer. Pip barely had time to squeal before a vine whipped out of the green and snapped around her ankle, and she was ripped clean off Britt's shoulder and yeeted back into the abyss of the forest. A quarter second later she came flying out again—this time in Bramble's grip, the plant-kin clutching both her shoulders and berating her faster than anyone had ever heard him speak. Why had she gone for the stacks? Bad idea, Pip. Bad idea. His eyes warred between throttling her and weeping with relief. Behind him drifted Saffron, quiet as ever, a face half-remembered from an old study group where she had done nothing but sketch.

Bramble caught up, skidded to a stop before them, and looked the squad over. "Thank you," he said, "for keeping stupid Pip alive."

"*Bard* was stupid," came Pip's indignant squeak—*I'm not stupid*—before Bramble looped a vine neatly around her mouth. "Hush, Pip. Your time for speaking and eating is suspended for the indefinite future." He wound her up against his torso and caged her there.

Aggie caught the shape of Bramble at the edge of her vision and went to say a quick hello—*you made it, but we've got to keep moving*—and in doing so came close to Val's grieving huddle. There she recognized the blonde hair of the one who'd been pimping out the potato in the arena, spilling from beneath one tarp, and the familiar spectacles of Finch resting atop the other. She understood then who the two dead were. Finch had been controversial—the rival who wouldn't share his notes, the one who'd tried to leverage a little insider trading—but Aggie only knew that grief was grief. She stopped before Val, and in the earnest, slightly-off cadence of a Mizizi trying hard to honor foreign custom, offered what she had. "I'm sorry for your loss," she said. Val's jaw tensed. He was working, visibly, not to be angry—swallowing something down. But it slipped out anyway, low and wrecked and not really aimed at her at all. "What is it *for?*" he said. "I don't have that answer right now."

They were following the tortoise across the beach when a blur of blue hair swept over Britt's eyes and she was caught up in a fierce hug that smelled faintly of river water. It was Real. Her sister squeezed her tight, half-laughing, half-frantic, saying she'd been asking everywhere — no one had seen a flare, no one at all. Had Britt not used it?

Real pulled back and stared at them, torn between exasperation and relief. They were idiots, she told them — idiots, and also brilliant, because they had survived when no one had any right to. The odds, she admitted, had not been great.

Real followed Britt's gaze and went still. Yeah, she said slowly, she knew that one — and she was glad they still had a sense of humor after everything. But then she blinked. *What?* And Britt remembered, then, that Real had only been with the clans for a year — though surely, she thought, she would have known about this. Real admitted she should. The *kasa* — she used the old clan word — yes, she recognized it. It was something she'd been taught to avoid at all costs. Why was it here? Should it even be here?

That settled something in Real's face — and hardened it. Then it was even more important, she said, that she get them to Professor Ink now. She started tugging at Britt's arm, steering them along the beach — not quite the tortoise's line, but offset from it — toward the pier vehicles where a tall walker stood among the docked hospital ships, a quill sigil painted on its flank. They had to talk to Ink, she insisted. This was crazy. This was part of Ink's whole theory.

No, Real said over her shoulder — but they had the stones.

There they found Professor Ink — a poised elven woman with raven-dark hair — while Rill spilled words in a frantic tumble, explaining that something impossible was happening, that in tens of thousands of years no tortoise had ever left its grove, and now one was walking through the forest, right there, and she'd already half-forgotten the details the elders had told her. Ink's hand lifted. *Calm. Slower. More clearly.* Even the professor admitted she wasn't sure she could describe it.

Ink introduced them properly — these were the two sisters Rill had spoken of, though only one could come, since the other was following the sacred tortoise through the camp. Ink strode forward in an elegant black suit, hand extended toward Britt. "It is a pleasure," she began, then reconsidered the corpses beyond the hull. "Well — maybe not today." Sensing Britt's hesitation, she offered instead the traditional Mizizi greeting, and they bumped fists.

Ink got to the point. She would select Britt's group, and at least one other crew, to guide her into the Mizi forest. She didn't yet know what they faced. Three days aboard Elijah — she gestured at the deck beneath her feet — the walker she had built to cross the Mizizi forest faster than anything alive. What had happened this night was unprecedented, and she would need a guide. "Would you come with me?"

"Great." Ink would meet them at the camp's edge in one hour and board. If Britt had anyone worth bringing, she could bring up to ten — that was all the walker and its crew could hold. Then Ink turned to her assistant. "Now, Rill — tell me everything you've learned on the ground so far."

In the settling calm of the op center, Rill crossed to where Zephyr lounged near Ignatius and allowed, stiffly, that she was glad Zephyr was alive — a courtesy she clearly did not entirely feel. Then her gaze slid past to Britt, and something in her face dropped. She swore under her breath: she'd totally forgotten. She needed Britt in the lab right now — this instant, fast as she could move — and she was already sprinting for the hatch and sliding down the ladder before she finished the sentence. Everyone near enough had heard it, and could follow if they chose.

Down in the lab, Rill ran to a heavy metal container in the corner and wrenched it open. From inside she drew a vial of glowing liquid — the very same color, Britt realized with a lurch, as the sample from the buried cache where they'd found the compass. Rill held it up. Did this look familiar?

Not good, Rill muttered, not good — sit, please, sit. She flipped out a second vial, this one neon purple, and pressed it toward Britt: she needed her to drink it immediately. Then, forcing herself steadier, she explained. She'd happened to be in the lab when the sample was brought in, and it had gutted her to recognize it — because this stuff came from where she'd come from, before she was Britt's sister, back before the exchange she still couldn't bring herself to talk about. The point, she said, was that Britt had somehow been exposed to a thing that grew only in the canyons where Rill had grown up, and it was lethal, and Rill couldn't remember how to cure it outright the way she once could. But if Britt drank this once a week, it would stall the disease — because otherwise, Britt, she said, you're going to die in about two weeks. She admitted she couldn't have managed even this without Professor Ink's help on the harmony medicine, and she knew Britt was still deciding where she drew her lines, but the longer she waited the less she'd get back of what she'd already lost, and it would not stop on its own.

Rill said she had no idea how that could even be possible; the stuff grew in exactly one part of the canyon, and no one ever went there.

That, Rill said, should not be possible either — that it could have appeared in the forest, that Rill herself hadn't been there when any of those afflicted showed symptoms. It was strange, deeply strange, and it should not be. Why would it be there at all? Why did it do the same thing to Britt that it did to the canyon-folk? Britt asked where it came from — whether it had been created, or merely gathered. It didn't come from anywhere, Rill said; it just grew. Then she rose, crossed the room, and quietly shut the door — leaving only Iggy, Aggie, Britt, and Rill, the four who had followed her down. Ignatius stood among them feeling the awkwardness of it, murmuring that he'd been so close for so long that it was hard to talk about being from a clan the exchange had scrubbed out of him; the indoctrination, he confessed, was something he was still overcoming.

Rill drew a breath and tried to be as honest as she could. She was from a clan they called the Wadi, she said, who lived in a canyon. Their spark — the thing that made them what they were — was a source of water that, her whole life, had been nothing but drips and trickles. Then, in the last few years, it had begun to surge and rise again, filling channels their people had always known were meant to hold it, until they'd had to rebuild the very houses they'd let crumble.

Not the time, Rill snapped — they were on a mystery hunt. But Ignatius pushed on: his own people had been dying out, had met with Harmony, and suddenly the magma and heat came surging back; now here was a society that revered death, connecting with Harmony, and finding more death in its midst. He didn't know if there was a link, but it nagged at him. They did not worship death, Rill corrected sharply. They acknowledged that death was the one inevitable truth, and that there had to be a necessary balance between life and death — you could not simply prevent it.

Ignatius agreed with her, in his roundabout way — perhaps maintaining balance had in fact thrown their balance off, perhaps Harmony had tipped it — but what he kept circling back to was the timeline. Did the sickness begin when they connected with Harmony, or before? The water didn't kill them, Rill insisted; the water was their life, their soul. Right, said Ignatius — so the water was rising, and people were falling ill, and were the two timelines aligned? Not for the Wadi, Rill said flatly. They didn't touch the stuff. They knew it was bad, radioactive, cursed; she hadn't even known it could exist anywhere but that cave. But here, she said, was what they did know: the last time this happened, the Mizizi said it was ten years ago — far before anyone had heard of Harmony, before Britt's clan was ever discovered by Vane, and long before the papermen came to the Mizizi.

Professor Ink came down the ladder into the lab barge already talking, half to herself and half to the room. She needed — she stopped, taking in the scene, then rounded on the nearest question that mattered. Had they given Britt the medicine yet? Was she cured? Not cured, someone said. Delayed. Delayed was good, the professor decided, and let out a breath.

Then she came to it in a rush, the shape of the thing turning over in her mind: their friend could see the turtles, they could all see the turtles — *we are turtles*, she said, mangling it in her excitement, but the point held. Everyone could see the creature. What no one could do was hold onto the memory of having seen it. She could keep her head straight in here, in the lab, where the grass was out of sight — but out there, the moment your eyes left it, the turtle simply erased itself from you.

They all did — all of them but Rill, who managed only a lopsided, groping *I remember talking about turtles, I think, sort of* before her certainty dissolved. The professor herself worried at the edge of it: in the lab she could nearly hold the thread, but only nearly, a memory that came apart the moment she gripped it. She hated it, she admitted — hated when her own mind was tampered with — and then, to steady herself, she pulled a scrap of paper from her coat and held it up. Across it, in a frantic scratching hand, she had written her instructions to her future forgetful self: *Don't look at turtle. Cadets can see turtle. Follow turtle.* She had meant, she said, to march them through the heart of the Mizi village, to sit with the elders and learn why they could no longer synchronize with the clan through the nodes the way Harmony connected to everyone else. But something in her insisted they trust the turtle instead — the fate of an empire riding on a walking shell, and it made no sense, and it felt right anyway. So. Any theories?

Their friend had been trapped inside it, Britt said — and, catching Lomi's eye across the barge, she told the rest, too: the memories they'd seen of people who'd broken the norms and died, the memories they themselves had somehow forgotten and only now recovered. The professor absorbed it all, then set it aside for later thought. If there was anything else, she told them, they should tell Rill, or her, or call Professor Kante — he liked biscuits, apparently; was that normal? So much they didn't know. She was already drifting toward the door when she pivoted back with one more question. Did they know any of the other clans? As far as she could tell they had Britt, and Zephyr, and Iggy — were there others? Rill couldn't remember. Could Lomi?
